name: Maya Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Maya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't take sides and we're not connected to any company, union or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a front-end loader on the ROM pad at Ironbark, an open-pit nickel mine. ROM means run-of-mine, it's the big stockpile area where the trucks dump ore before it goes into the crusher. I blend the ore, feeding the crusher the right mix of high and low grade so the plant runs smoothly. It's a bit like cooking, you learn the colours of the rock. Twelve-hour shifts, five days on, four off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the plant guys rely on me. If I get the blend wrong, I hear about it on the radio within the hour. What wears me out is nights, and the fact that Daniel (my husband) is an electrician at Ironbark too, so when our rosters don't line up we barely see each other. We're at church on Sundays when we can be, and that keeps us sane.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Is anything at the mine on your mind at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nickel prices, mostly. Last year there was talk of Ironbark going into care and maintenance, which means shutting down and just keeping the site ticking over until prices recover. It didn't happen, but both our pays come from that one mine. We've got about seven months of savings and a block of land, so we're not desperate, but it sits in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a relief, honestly. We've got enough to think about with the nickel price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that people got carried away. At work we'd joke that the clever computers still can't blend ore like me. I don't really post online, maybe on the church group if someone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the real worry is still the nickel price, not robots. If the nickel mine goes quiet, Daniel (my husband) and I both lose our pay on the same day. That's a bigger risk to us than any chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving. I'd push Daniel to apply at the gold mine down the road, so we're not both at Ironbark. And we'd hold off on building on the block until nickel picks up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not because of AI. Because of where we both work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned starting a family. Does this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd love to start a family in the next two years. But I'm not stepping back from work until we know the mine is safe for a while. Maybe a year later than we hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Daniel and not you, for moving mines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's the one with the easier move. Electricians get work anywhere, at the gold mine, in town, even on farms. A loader driver needs a mine.

say: People got **carried away**, and she'd be glad it settled down.
Computers still can't **blend ore** like an experienced loader driver.
think: The real worry is the **nickel price**, not robots.
If Ironbark goes quiet, she and Daniel **both lose pay** at once.
do: Push Daniel to apply at the **gold mine** so they're not both at Ironbark.
Hold off **building on the block** until nickel prices pick up.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, because both their incomes come from one mine.
S0.quote: If the nickel mine goes quiet, Daniel (my husband) and I both lose our pay on the same day.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **household concentration**, not AI.
She'd delay a **first child** by about a year until the mine looks safe.
She sees **Daniel's trade** as more portable than her own.

steps.text: Keep blending ore on the ROM pad at Ironbark
Save hard and hold off building on the block
Get Daniel to apply for electrician work at the gold mine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots slowly in hands-on work. That's my side of the line, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly the office people who'll feel it, and that we should help them, not laugh at them. Somebody still has to blend the ore. But I'd say it carefully, because some of them are friends from church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the loader on the ROM pad is one of the easier jobs to automate. It's the same patch of ground every day. They're already putting sensors on the stockpiles, and the AI tells me the grades now. Five years from now, a remote loader is pretty likely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new grade software properly, once a couple of the others have tried it and it works. I'd ask about the remote loader trial when it comes, because I'd rather run it from a chair than watch someone else do it. And we'd keep saving, maybe a thousand a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not a disaster, it's a change, and I don't love change but I can handle it if I see it working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until it's proven. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't be the first one, don't be the last one. Wait till it's proven, then get in properly. That's how my mum ran her bakery and it worked for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame the companies a bit, they only care about cost. But honestly it's their business and their money. My job is to make sure I'm worth keeping.

say: The **office people** will feel it first and deserve help, not jokes.
She'd speak **carefully** because some are friends from church.
think: The **ROM pad loader** is one of the easier jobs to automate.
A **remote loader** is likely within five years at Ironbark.
do: Learn the **grade software** once others show it works.
Ask to join the **remote loader trial** when it comes.
feel: **Uneasy**; she doesn't love change but can handle it once it's proven.
S1.quote: Don't be the first one, don't be the last one. Wait till it's proven, then get in properly.
fieldNote: Her rule for change comes from her **mum's bakery**, a family lesson.
She takes **personal responsibility** rather than blaming the company.
She sees her own job as **easy to automate**, which is honest.

steps.text: Learn the new stockpile grade software after others test it
Apply for the remote loader trial at Ironbark
Save about a thousand dollars a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. That's a lot. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and the companies have let this run away from them. Nobody asked the people it lands on. At church I'd ask people to look out for each other, because a lot of families will be hit at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think both our jobs go. The thinking side runs the mine by 2028, and by 2031 the robots can do my loader and probably Daniel's wiring too. If Ironbark goes fully automated, there's no fallback in the other mines either, because they'll do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, Daniel and I sit down with the savings and the block of land. We'd sell the block, I think, and keep the cash. I'd keep working every shift until the robots arrive, and in those three years I'd train for something with people in it, maybe aged care, which my aunt does. We'd put the baby off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put the baby off. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest bit. We've wanted a baby since we got married. But I won't bring a baby into a house with no income and no plan. We'd wait, and we'd pray about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it all went wrong, who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably family. My parents have a spare room, and Daniel's brother has a farm. We wouldn't need government money if we had family, and I'd rather that.

say: Governments and companies **let this run away** without asking anyone.
She'd ask the **church** to look out for families hit at once.
think: **Both their jobs** go: her loader and Daniel's wiring.
Other mines offer **no fallback** because they'd automate too.
do: Sell **the block** of land and keep the cash.
Work every shift while training for **aged care** in the three-year gap.
Put off having **a baby** until there's income and a plan.
S2.quote: I won't bring a baby into a house with no income and no plan.
fieldNote: Both earners at **one mine** turns AGI into a household-wide threat.
She uses the **robot gap** to train for aged care, work with people in it.
She turns to **family and faith** before government.

steps.text: Sell the block of land and keep the money as cash
Train in aged care while still driving the loader
Put off trying for a baby with Daniel
Fall back on her parents' spare room if pay stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. Still fast, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this gives us time if we use it. I'd say it to the younger women on my crew especially, get a second skill now. I'd still say the companies owe the towns something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get until about 2034 on the loader, so seven years. Daniel would probably last a bit longer, someone has to fix the robots for a while. That's time to have a baby and get set up, if we're careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the block and build a smaller house on it, nothing fancy. I'd do the aged care certificate part-time over two years, so I have it when I need it. And Daniel would move to the gold mine, so we're not both at Ironbark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. But it's the kind I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still put the baby off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think we'd go ahead with the baby, maybe in a year. Seven years of good pay is a lot, and we'd have a plan B. My mum had me when she was twenty-eight and the bakery was struggling, and she managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in your usual way of doing things, here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waiting too long. I'm good at waiting till things are proven, but with AI the proof comes when it's too late. I'd have to make myself start the course this year.

She'd tell younger women on her crew to get a **second skill** now.
think: She gets about **seven years** on the loader, until around 2034.
Daniel lasts longer, as someone must **fix the robots**.
do: Build a **smaller house** on the block instead of selling it.
Study an **aged care certificate** part-time over two years.
Move Daniel to the **gold mine** to split their risk.

S3.quote: I'm good at waiting till things are proven, but with AI the proof comes when it's too late.
fieldNote: She spots that her **wait-for-proof** habit fails with a deadline.
Five years lets the **baby plan** go ahead within a year.
Splitting the household across **two mines** is her main safeguard.

steps.text: Study an aged care certificate part-time over two years
Build a smaller house on the block and try for a baby
Move Daniel to electrician work at the gold mine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Probably two kids by then, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but don't waste it waiting for someone else to plan. I'd tell people to look at what their kids should study, not just their own jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine for most of it. I'd do the loader until the kids are in school, then move into something else around 2033. The worry is more for the kids, what they'll do for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd build the house and start the family next year. I'd use the remote loader software when it comes in, because by then it'll be proven. And I'd save for the kids' education, a set amount each month, maybe four hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled. It feels like ordinary planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel say about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel would say we're fine, he always does. Daniel's dad said the same about the cattle prices, and he lost half the herd. So I'd still be the one with the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade, probably, or nursing. Something with hands and people together. I'd never push my kids into mining like my dad pushed me, but I wouldn't stop them either.

People should think about what **their kids** should study, not just their own jobs.

The real worry moves to **the kids' future** work.
do: Build the house and **start a family** next year.
Use the **remote loader** software once it's proven.
Save about **four hundred** a month for the kids' education.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both our jobs go at once and there's no time to have a baby and get set up. What would help is if the mine had to train people before automating, and if trades and aged care courses were local and cheap, so I could study between shifts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples who work at the same place. Lots of mining families are like us. When the mine sneezes, the whole house catches a cold.

headlineQuote: Lots of mining families are like us. When the mine sneezes, the whole house catches a cold.
portrait: Maya, 27, runs a **front-end loader** blending ore at Ironbark, an open-pit nickel mine.
She is married to **Daniel**, an electrician at the same mine, so one site pays them both.
She is **careful and faithful**, waiting until change is proven, and plans a family soon.
**AGI by 2028** alarms her because both jobs go and the baby plan would stop.
With more warning she'd train in **aged care** and move Daniel to another mine.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when both household jobs go at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Local, cheap courses** in trades and aged care to study between shifts.
